title: Logger Rate Limiter
statement:
Build a class `Logger` that receives a stream of log messages, each stamped with a time in seconds, and throttles repeats: after a message is printed at time `t`, the identical message text may not be printed again until time `t + 10`.

- `Logger()` creates a logger that has printed nothing yet.
- `shouldPrintMessage(timestamp, message)` returns `true` when `message` has never been printed or was last printed at `timestamp - 10` or earlier; that call counts as printing `message` at `timestamp`. Otherwise it returns `false`, and the refused call changes nothing.

Different messages are throttled independently. Calls arrive in chronological order (timestamps never decrease), and several calls may share the same timestamp.
constraints: Timestamps are passed in non-decreasing order
At most 10^4 calls are made to shouldPrintMessage
notes:
## Intuition

Each call only cares about one thing: when was this exact message last printed? Scanning a list of every earlier print answers that, but costs O(number of prints) per call. A hash map keyed by the message answers it in O(1). Instead of storing the last print time, store the first time the message may print again, `timestamp + 10`; then the test is a single comparison.

## Approach

1. Keep a map `nextAllowed` from each printed message to the earliest timestamp at which it may be printed again.
2. On `shouldPrintMessage(timestamp, message)`, look up `allowedAt = nextAllowed.get(message)`.
3. If the message has an entry and `timestamp < allowedAt`, it is still blocked: return `false` without touching the map.
4. Otherwise it prints: set `nextAllowed[message] = timestamp + 10` and return `true`.

## Example 1, step by step

- `(1, "foo")`: no entry, so print; `nextAllowed` is `{foo: 11}`. Returns `true`.
- `(2, "bar")`: no entry, so print; `{foo: 11, bar: 12}`. Returns `true`.
- `(3, "foo")`: `3 < 11`, blocked. Returns `false`.
- `(8, "bar")`: `8 < 12`, blocked. Returns `false`.
- `(10, "foo")`: `10 < 11`, blocked. Returns `false`.
- `(11, "foo")`: `11` is not below `11`, so print; `foo` becomes `21`. Returns `true`.

With `null` for the constructor, the output is `[null, true, true, false, false, false, true]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(L) per call to hash a message of length L (at most 30), effectively O(1).
- Space: O(M · L) for M distinct messages ever printed.

## Pitfalls

- A refused call must not update the map; otherwise a message sent every 5 seconds would be blocked forever.
- The window is exclusive at the end: a message printed at `t` may print again at exactly `t + 10`, so the test is `timestamp < allowedAt`, not `<=`.
- The map keeps every distinct message forever. When memory matters, a queue of recent prints can evict entries older than 10 seconds, which relies on timestamps arriving in order.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `nextAllowed` | map from a message to the first timestamp at which it may print again |
| `timestamp`, `message` | the current call's time and text |
| `allowedAt` | this message's entry in `nextAllowed`, or `undefined` if it was never printed |

narration.3: nextAllowed maps each printed message to the first time it may print again.
narration.7: Look up when this exact message is next allowed; undefined means it was never printed.
narration.8: A known message whose waiting time has not passed yet is still blocked...
narration.9: ...so refuse it and leave the map unchanged.
narration.11: The message prints now, so it is blocked until 10 seconds from now.
narration.12: Tell the caller to print it.
